question_text: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of worsening nocturia, fatigue, and shortness of breath on exertion. While he used to be able to walk for 15 minutes at a time, he now has to pause every 5 minutes. Recently, he has started using two pillows to avoid waking up short of breath at night. He has a history of hypertension treated with daily amlodipine and prazosin; he has difficulty adhering to his medication regimen. His pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a laterally displaced apical heartbeat and 2+ bilateral pitting edema of the lower legs. Auscultation shows an S4 gallop and fine bibasilar rales. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following pathophysiologic changes in this patient?

                    ### Question

While he used to be able to walk for 15 minutes at a time, he now has to pause every 5 minutes. Recently, he has started using two pillows to avoid waking up short of breath at night. He has a history of hypertension treated with daily amlodipine and prazosin; he has difficulty adhering to his medication regimen. His pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a laterally displaced apical heartbeat and 2+ bilateral pitting edema of the lower legs. Auscultation shows an S4 gallop and fine bibasilar rales. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following pathophysiologic changes in this patient?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms and examination findings are consistent with heart failure, likely heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) due to hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy. In heart failure, decreased cardiac output leads to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which causes constriction of efferent renal arterioles to maintain glomerular filtration rate. This aligns with the consensus that heart failure often results in increased RAAS activity and renal compensatory mechanisms. The evidence path 'Heart failure'-CAUSES/COMPLICATES->'Pulmonary congestion' supports the presence of pulmonary congestion, as indicated by bibasilar rales and orthopnea. The chain suggesting 'Retention of potassium' is incorrect, as heart failure typically leads to sodium and water retention, not potassium retention. The chain suggesting 'Decrease in total peripheral vascular resistance' is also incorrect, as heart failure often results in increased peripheral vascular resistance due to sympathetic activation. The correct pathophysiologic change in this patient is the 'Constriction of efferent renal arterioles' due to RAAS activation.
